claims.text: Conventional preparation of single-phase ZrB2 requires sintering above 2300 °C.
Conventionally sintered ZrB2 exhibits incomplete densification and residual porosity.
Residual porosity in ZrB2 increases susceptibility to defects caused by liquid plating-bath exposure.
SPS can produce single-phase ZrB2 below 2300 °C.
SPS can densify ZrB2 at approximately 2000–2100 °C.
SPS permits shorter sintering times for ZrB2 than conventional processing.
SPS enhances ZrB2 densification and reduces grain-boundary porosity.
Reduced grain-boundary porosity minimizes the formation of microstructural holes.
Pulsed electric current during SPS produces localized Joule heating in ZrB2.
Localized heating during SPS promotes rapid diffusion and lower-temperature sintering.
Rapid SPS densification limits grain coarsening and porosity associated with prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Porosity and related defects act as sites for liquid penetration during plating.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will have lower porosity than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will have mechanical integrity comparable to or better than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will undergo less degradation during long-term liquid plating-bath exposure.
The cited high-entropy oxide study used SPS as a faster and scalable alternative to a previously slower preparation technique.
SPS benefits observed in a Co-Cr-Fe-Mn-Ni oxide may scale to ZrB2.
The optimal SPS temperature, pressure, and dwell time for fully densifying ZrB2 without adverse effects are not established.
The experiment compares composition-matched conventional and SPS ZrB2 specimens using microstructure, porosity, density, strength, and post-exposure defect measurements.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in porosity, defect density, or post-exposure mechanical degradation would falsify the hypothesis.
